Exploration of biomass fractionation and lignin removal for enhancing enzymatic digestion of wheat-stalk through deep eutectic solvent Cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride:Lactic acid treatment
Ying Chen⁰, Zhengyu Tang⁰, Wei Tang⁰, Cuiluan Maⁱ, Yu-Cai He⁰,*

ª *School of Pharmacy & Biological and Food Engineering, Changzhou University, Changzhou 213164, China* b *State Key Laboratory of Biocatalysis and Enzyme Engineering, Hubei University, Wuhan 430062, China*
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Lignocellulose pretreatment Delignification Enzymolysis

ABSTRACT The cationic surfactant-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted extensive attention due to their effectual destruction of the natural anti-degradation barrier structure in lignocellulose. In this research, functional DES Cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride: Lactic acid (CTAC:LA molar ratio 1:0.5 to 1:6) was fabricated for pretreating wheat-stalk. The relationships of accessibility, lignin removal, xylan separation, and enzymolysis efficiency were explored. The highest delignification (88.3%) and xylan removal (89.0%) were obtained through the treatment with CTAC:LA (1:4, mol/mol, 160 °C, 60 min), acquiring 86.8% of enzymolysis efficiency. The structure of CTAC:LA-treated wheat-stalk was changed to porous state, while the accessibility and crystallinity were substantially improved to 668.2 mg/g and 57.6%, respectively. The lignin surface area declined from 672.7 to 335.4 m²/g. Furthermore, the structure of lignin disrupted by CTAC:LA was analyzed by 2D-HSQC NMR, implying that CTAC:LA could cleave the C-O covalent bond and C-C bond and degrade the S- and H-units in wheat-stalk lignin through interaction. The potential pretreatment mechanism was proposed through comprehensive exploration at the molecular level and macro level, and this built pretreatment process held great promise for valorizing biomass into highly valuable chemicals.

## 1. Introduction Under the double pressure of global energy crisis and environmental pollution issue, seeking effectual and eco-friendly energy production mode has become a research hotspot in modern society [1]. Wheat-stalk (WS) is a common agricultural waste, rendering as an important feed-stock for producing chemicals and fuels in biorefinery [2,3]. However, in the complex structure of WS, lignin combines with hemicelluloses to fabricate the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC), shielding cellulose accessible surface, blocking the cell wall deconstruction and hindering enzymolysis [4]. Distinct from cellulose and lignin, hemicellulose is prone to degradation under high temperature [5]. Lignin is known as a polyphenol biomacromolecule with complex structure [6]. It has a random three-dimensional structure formed by covalent cross-linking of multiple subunits, and the complexity of these connections makes lignin difficult to degrade [7,8]. Consequently, it is of great significance to disrupt lignin and hemicellulose in lignocellulose through efficient pretreatment, greatly improving its enzymolysis efficiency.

In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs), which can be fabricated by mixing hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD), have gained extensive attentions as a new green solvent for breaking down and hydrolyzing LCC through the disruption of the existing bonding interactions between carbohydrates and lignin [9,10]. Alvarez-Vasco et al. used four DESs (ChCl:Lactic acid, ChCl:Acetic acid, ChCl:Levulinic acid, and ChCl:Glycerol) for extraction of lignin in poplar wood. Among all four DESs, ChCl:Lactic acid had the greatest effect on lignin removal [11]. It has been reported that the enhanced lignin removal effect of ChCl:Lactic acid could be attributed to the high hydrogen bond supply capacity of lactic acid (LA), which makes the ether bonds in lignin easy to crack during the removal of lignin [12]. Recently, cationic surfactants with hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties have been used to reduce surface tension of lignocellulose driving the removal of hydrophobic molecules such as lignin, thus affecting the enzymolysis efficiency of lignocellulose [13], and they were used to synthesize DESs for removing lignin and enhancing enzymatic saccharification. Using CTAB and ethylene glycol to synthesize DES for the pre- treatment of rape straw, the lignin removal reached 62.2%, resulting in a 46.0% of enzymolysis efficiency [15]. However, the pretreatment ability of CTAB-based DES containing Br- is not ideal, and exploring high efficiency of surfactant-based DES for efficiently removing lignin and promoting enzymolysis has gained great attention. In addition, the corresponding mechanism for lignin elimination and enhanced enzy- molysis through the DES pretreatment need to be well interpreted.

It has been reported that the supplementary of CI- into the pre-treatment system can significantly increase the lignin elimination [9,16] and destroy lignocellulose structure [17]. In addition, chloride can participate in stabilizing the protonation transition state of the acid-catalyzed reaction [18]. Therefore, cationic surfactant-based DESS containing CI- group might be efficiently used for efficient biomass pretreatment and valorization. Accordingly, cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride (CTAC), as CI--contained surfactant, was utilized as HBA to fabricate novel surfactant-based DES CTAC:LA by using lactic acid (LA) as HBD, which was used as an eco-friendly and efficient solvent for WS pretreatment in this research. The impact of pretreatment parameters such as DES CTAC:LA solvent properties, CTAC-to-LA molar ratio, pre-treatment temperature, and pretreatment duration on biomass frac-tionation efficiency were assessed. Meanwhile, the contents of furfural and XOSs and the effects of reaction severity factors on their formation were analyzed. The alterations in the chemical composition, surface microstructure, crystal structure, accessibility, and surface lignin area of WS through the CTAC:LA treatment were interpreted by a range of characterization methods (XRD, SEM, dye adsorption techniques, etc.). Additionally, two-dimensional heteronuclear single quantum coherent nuclear magnetic resonance (2D-HSQC NMR) was applied to analyze the changes of lignin structure. The CTAC:LA treatment mechanism for enhancing the enzymolysis of WS was explored and discussed. These efforts comprehensively elaborated the CTAC:LA treatment mechanism, deepened the understanding of the structural characteristics of lignin, and provided scientific basis for promoting lignocellulose pretreatment efficiency in biorefining.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Chemicals and materials The wheat-stalk (WS) used in the experiment was collected from Jiangsu, China. The substrates were ground to 20–60 mesh. Cetyl tri- methyl ammonium chloride (CTAC) were purchased from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co. Ltd. Lactic acid (AR) and other chemicals were sourced from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., LTD.

2.2. Preparation of *CTAC:LA* and related parameters DES was fabricated by cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride (HBA) and lactic acid (HBD) at different HBA:HBD molar ratios (from 1:0.5 to 1:6), the surface tension was measured with surface tensimeter (KINO A201, U.S.A.), the viscosity was measured with rotary viscometer (Brookfield A1017, U.S.A.), and the average was repeated three times. The synthesis of DES (CTAC:LA) was verified by FT-IR. The hydrogen bond capacity of DESs was quantified by Kamlet-Taft solvation parameters, and hydrogen bond donor capacity (α), hydrogen bond acceptor capacity (β), and polarity/polarizability (π*) were determined as previously described [19].
2.3. Pretreatment and chemical composition analysis of WS DES and WS were mixed at a specific solid-liquid mass ratio (1:15) in a 250-mL flask, which was immersed in oil bath. The pretreatment was

implemented with DES (molar ratio of HBA-to-HBD 1:0.5-1:6) at a designed reaction temperature (120 °C-200 °C) for a certain pretreat- ment duration (20 min-100 min). The pretreatment severity factor (LogR0) serves as a comprehensive parameter for assessing the intensity of biomass pretreatment processes, and this factor typically considers the effects of temperature and time during pretreatment on reaction strength. It has proven to be an effective tool for comparing and pre- dicting the performance of various pretreatment strategies in terms of hemicellulose dissolution and lignin removal [20]. Based on the given reaction temperature (T) and time (t), LogR0 (the severity factor) was defined according to Eq. (1). The pretreated WS samples obtained from the different severity factor were used for chemical composition analysis and enzymolysis.

According to the analytical method provided by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory of the United States, the biomass chem- ical composition (glucan, xylan, and lignin) was determined. 2.4. *Enzymolysis of WS* Raw WS or WS after pretreatment were hydrolyzed with cellulase (10 FPU/g-glucan) in citric acid buffer solution (pH 4.8, 50 mM) to test enzymolysis efficiency. The hydrolysis reaction was implemented at 50 °C for 72 h. The supernatant was subsequently sampled to determine the monosaccharide content. Enzymolysis efficiency (EE) was calculated using the following formula:
EE (%) = ([Glucose] + [cellobiose] in enzymatic hydrolysate (g) × 0.9) / (Glucan in pretreated WS (g)) × 100 (5)

2.5. *Quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations* To gain a deeper understanding of the interactions between the typical structural units [S- (syringyl), G- (guaiacyl), and H- (p-hydroxyphenyl) types] of WS lignin and CTAC:LA solvent systems, the interaction types were visually differentiated based on the independent gradient model (IGM) in density functional theory (DFT) to reveal the strong non-covalent interactions between atoms or molecules in the system [21]. Additionally, visual molecular dynamics (VMD) was utilized to draw electrostatic potential (ESP) and other color mapping isosurfaces to visualize the trajectory data of the system [22].

## 2.8. Recovery and reuse of the DES The recycling ability of DES is an important index of its biomass pretreatment performance [14]. Firstly, WS was pretreated with CTAC: LA (HBA:HBD molar ratio = 1:4) at 160 °C at a 1:15 of solid-liquid mass ratio for 60 min. After the reaction, the pretreated liquid was filtered using filter bottle and Brinell funnel. Then the filtrate was repeatedly used as a solvent for the next run of pretreatment, which was carried out under the same biomass conditions. The filter residue was rinsed and utilized for subsequent component analysis and enzymolysis.

2.9. _Statistical analysis_ All the pretreatment and enzymolysis experiments were implemented in triplicate to confirm the reproducibility of the data. The SPSS software was utilized for the analysis of variance (ANOVA) to test for statistically significant differences.

### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Investigation of HBA:HBD molar ratio on affecting the enzymolysis The molar ratio of HBA to HBD in DES can affect the solubility and selective dissolution of biomass components [29]. It was found that the total lignin content (acid-soluble lignin + acid-insoluble lignin) reached

14.6 % (Fig. 1a), the lignin removal only reached 51.4 %, and the enzymolysis efficiency was 49.4 % after CTAC:LA (HBA:HBD = 1:0.5, 160 °C, 60 min) treatment (Fig. 1b). It was reported that a low pro-portion of HBD couldn't form effective hydrogen-bond network and resulted in increased viscosity and reduced fluidity of the solvent, which would impact the dissolution efficiency between the solvent and biomass [30]. When the CTAC-to-LA molar ratio reached 1:4, the xylan removal (89.0 %) and lignin removal (88.3 %) reached their highest value, acquiring 86.8 % of enzymolysis efficiency. As the CTAC-to-LA molar ratio continued to increase to 1:6, the lignin removal showed a weak downward trend (from 88.3 % to 86.5 %), and the enzymolysis efficiency also declined correspondingly (Fig. 1b). Simultaneously, it has been demonstrated that the molar ratio of HBA to HBD significantly impacted the enzymolysis efficiency through statistical data analysis (p < 0.05) (Table S1, see supplementary file). Continuing to increase the molar ratio of HBA:HBD might improve the polarity of DESs and weaken its interaction with non-polar or hydrophobic biomass components, such as lignin, thereby reducing DES's ability to dissolve lignocellulose [31]. Therefore, CTAC:LA = 1:4 was considered the most appropriate HBA: HBD molar ratio.

By using LA as HBD, the absorption peak of LA's carboxyl group was red-shifted, as shown in FT-IR spectra. Meanwhile, the bending vibra-tion of quaternary ammonium cation in CTAC also changed (Fig. S1, see supplementary file). The frequency shift and intensity changes of the representative bands of CTAC and LA in FT-IR spectra confirmed the existence of molecular hydrogen bonds between CTAC and LA [32], implying the successful synthesis of DES. The Kamlet-Taft solvation parameters of DES solvent can be used to evaluate its solubility [33]. With increasing the molar ratio of HBA:HBD, the π* value remained between 0.20 and 0.27, the β value of the solvent (Lewis alkalinity) remained between 1.13 and 1.20, manifesting great hydrogen bond acceptance capacity of CTAC. The α value of the solvent (Lewis acidity) elevated from 0.36 to 1.77, and the hydrogen bond donor capacity changed with the HBA:HBD molar ratio (from 1:0.5 to 1:6) (Table S2, see supplementary file). It was also found that there were fittings about the α value and the solubility of lignin and xylan. As displayed in Fig. 1c, the xylan removal [Y(Xylan removal) = 46.93 × X(Hydrogen bond acidity) + 31.12, R² = 0.86] and delignification [Y(Delignification) = 39.34 × X(Hydrogen bond acidity) + 39.76, R² = 0.91] were positively correlated with the α value of DES. Higher α value in the solvent facilitated the elimination of lignin and xylan because it might enhance the hydrogen-bond interaction be-tween the solvent and lignocellulose, making it easier for the lignin and xylan to dissociate from the biomass complex [34].

The viscosity and surface tension of the solvent can directly affect its diffusion rate and permeability in lignocellulosic pores [35]. CTAC is a cationic surfactant with molecular structure that includes hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail, giving it the ability to reduce surface tension [36]. As showcased in Table 1, solvent systems with different CTAC:LA molar ratios all exhibited low surface tension (29.1–30.9 mN/m), which facilitated CTAC:LA in effectually wetting solid surfaces, penetrating biomass fibers more easily, and promoting the separation of lignocellulosic components. When the CTAC:LA molar ratio reached 1:2, the high viscosity (1223.1 cP) limited the effective contact between the solvent and the biomass. As the molar ratio of CTAC:LA was increased to 1:4, the viscosity was reduced to 380.9 cP, and the removal of lignin and xylan elevated apparently. This was because DESs with lower viscosity could penetrate into the biomass structure more quickly, improving mass transfer performance and efficiency [37].

Accordingly, the impact of two key parameters in the severity factor (pretreatment temperature and duration) on the pretreatment effectiveness was assessed and optimized.

As shown in Tables S3 & S4 (see supplementary files), the statistical data analysis implied that both pretreatment temperature and reaction duration significantly influenced enzymolysis efficiency (p < 0.05). Upon undergoing pretreatment temperature from 120 °C to 160 °C, there was significant decrease in lignin content (acid-soluble lignin + acid-insoluble lignin) in WS from 18.5% to 8.0%, and a decrease in xylan content from 15.1% to 8.1% (Fig. 2a). This resulted in substantial increase in the lignin removal (from 33.4% to 84.3%) and xylan removal (from 41.7% to 83.0%), while enzymolysis efficiency elevated from 49.4% to 80.1% (Fig. 2b). According to the Fig. 2b, the delignification increased from 84.3% to 91.2%, but the trend of improvement in enzymolysis efficiency was no longer obvious as the pretreatment
temperature increased from 160 °C to 180 °C. Based on the above re-sults, 160 °C was considered to be the most appropriate reaction temperature.

According to Fig. 2c & d, upon raising reaction duration from 20 min to 60 min, the lignin content (acid-soluble lignin + acid-insoluble lignin) decreased from 15.6 % to 8.0 %, the lignin removal elevated from 37.6 % to 84.3 %, the xylan removal rose from 50.5 % to 83.0 %, and the enzymolysis efficiency was raised from 55.8 % to 80.1 %. However, with the continuous increase of reaction duration (from 60 min to 100 min) and pretreatment temperature (from 180 °C to 200 °C), the enzymolysis efficiency still manifested downward trend, although the xylan separation and lignin removal were slightly increased. This phenomenon was associated with the fact that higher temperatures and prolonged pretreatment duration might accelerate biomass degradation and produce more by-products, and excessive by-products will bind to the surface of the material with other degradations, inhibiting the digestion of lignocellulose with cellulases [39]. Consequently, severity factor of 3.54 (160 °C, 60 min) was deemed the optimal factor for the CTAC:LA treatment of WS.

Xylo-oligosaccharides (XOSs) and furfural are valuable products that can be derived from biomass in the pretreatment process [42,43]. In this research, the relationship between the content of XOSs and furfural in the pretreatment solution with the severity factor by adjustment of pretreatment temperature and duration was investigated. As the severity factor elevated from 2.36 to 3.54, the xylan degradation led to an increase in XOSs production from 0.6 g/L to 2.3 g/L. However, excessively high temperatures and longer reaction duration might lead to further degradation of XOSs into xylose, demonstrating an inverse "hook-shape" fitting [Y(Xylo-oligosaccharides) = -0.60 × X^3 + 5.72 × X^2 - 16.36 × X(Log R0) + 15.23, R^2 = 0.82] between the content of XOSs and severity factors

(Fig. 3c). Furfural, as an important and versatile chemical intermediate, is acquired through the dehydration of xylose in acidic environment at high temperatures [44]. It could be seen from Fig. 3c that there was positive fitting between the severity factors and furfural production [Y(Furfural) = 3.21 × X(Log R0) -8.56, R2 = 0.84]. With increasing severity factors from 2.96 to 4.72, the formed furfural could increase from 0.5 g/L to 6.0 g/L.

### 3.4. Molecular dynamics simulation Molecular dynamics simulation is able to render atomic and molec-ular level insights by simulating the interactions between substrate and solvent molecules [50]. In this research, the interactions between the CTAC:LA treatment system and lignin were discussed by molecular dy-namics simulation. The lignin in WS is a typical S-G-H type lignin (Syringyl-Guaiacyl-p-Hydroxyphenyl lignin). To further understand the

interaction between the lignin unit and the CTAC:LA treatment system, the weak interaction between the CTAC:LA and the lignin structure was visualized. Van der Waals forces, which mainly include electrostatic interaction, induction force and dispersion force, might promote the interaction between pretreatment solvents and non-polar or hydropho- bic compounds in lignocellulose, and promote their degradation [51]. In molecular simulations, electrostatic interactions can be evaluated by electrostatic potential. Among the three lignin structural models, G-type lignin model molecules manifested the strongest electrostatic interac- tion with DES, since the lowest self-electrostatic potential value of -0.961 (Fig. 5a). The hydroxy hydrogen atoms of lignin have a positive electrostatic potential, while the hydroxy oxygen atoms have the opposite. 3.7. Mass flow and energy flow Lignocellulose can be effectually transformed into fermentable sugars and other bio-based products through efficient pretreatment and enzymolysis [62,63]. After CTAC:LA fractionation, the cellulose-rich solid residue consisting of 212.0 g glucan, 18.1 g xylan, 17.2 g acid-insoluble lignin, and 3.4 g acid-soluble lignin was recovered. The removal of xylan was 89.0 % and the lignin removal reached 88.3 %. In the pretreatment liquid, 38.9 g furfural and 34.0 g xylo-oligosaccharides were produced. After enzymolysis of the cellulose-rich solid residue, 201.9 g glucose, 2.5 g cellobiose, 14.5 g xylose, 1.1 g arabinose were released (Fig. 8a). These sugars are important bio-based products that can be used in subsequent biotransformation processes. To explore the potential applications of this biorefining pathway, the overall energy flow was further evaluated (Fig. 8b). The energy flow image manifested that the high calorific value (HHV) of WS consists of glucan (7.26 MJ/kg WS), xylan (2.87 MJ/kg WS), and lignin (4.26 MJ/kg WS). Throughout the entire biorefining process of WS (1000 g), the energy output of furfural, XOSs, and lignin-enriched products reached 0.91, 0.60, and 5.30 MJ respectively. The majority of carbohydrate energy has been successfully converted into value-added forms, demonstrating the potential industrial application. Despite the remarkable progress in the biomass utilization and conversion process, the generation of lignin-enriched products after pretreatment was still an unavoidable problem. Lignin has the potential for many applications [64]. Li et al. found that the lignin regenerated from the acid DES (ChCl:oxalic acid) pretreatment solution had good thermal stability and antioxidant activity [65]. In addition, Liu et al. showed that biobased plastics prepared with recycled lignin from the pretreatment solution have better mechanical and tensile strength [66]. Therefore, these lignin-rich products generated in the CTAC:LA pretreatment system provide unlimited possibilities for further processing and upgrading into high value-added products (such as antioxidants, heat stabilizers, and plastics).

3.8. _Potential CTAC:LA pretreatment mechanism_ Effective pretreatment of WS was realized through the action of DES (CTAC:LA), and its potential pretreatment mechanism was illustrated in Fig. 9. As a carboxylic acid with high hydrogen bond donor capacity, lactic acid might provide large numbers of protons for efficient elimi- nation of hemicellulose and lignin [12]. CTAC, a surfactant with hy- drophobic long alkyl chain structure, not only affected the hydrophobic

lignin structure but also could prevent the decomposed lignin molecules from recondensing into pseudo-lignin and being deposited on the biomass surface [53]. Under the action of CTAC:LA treatment system, a large number of lignin and xylan were eliminated from the WS structure, which substantially elevated the accessibility and crystallinity of WS after treatment, and reduced the lignin surface area, thus advancing the subsequent enzymolysis efficiency (Fig. 9). Through quantum chemistry calculation and molecular dynamics simulation, it was found that there was strong and weak interaction (mainly van der Waals forces and hydrogen bond interaction) between lignin model and CTAC:LA treat- ment system. These interactions lead to the weakened connections be- tween lignin, hemicellulose and cellulose, and the S-units, H-units, C—O (β-0-4) covalent and C—C (β-5, β-β) bonds in the lignin were effectually cleaved by CTAC:LA, promoting the removal of lignin and thereby enhancing the enzymolysis of carbohydrates.

The key to making the most of lignocellulose and achieving an environmentally sustainable future lies in effective pretreatment strategies [67-69]. In this research, CTAC containing CI- was used as hydrogen bond receptor to synthesize a new type of cationic surfactant-based DES (CTAC:LA). This system could efficiently remove lignin and xylan from WS, significantly improve the accessibility and crystallinity of WS after pretreatment and make the substrate after pretreatment show excellent enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency (86.8%). This provided favorable conditions for the conversion of biomass into high-value chemicals. In addition, various characterizations combined with molecular simulation revealed the potential pretreatment mechanism of cationic surfactant-based DES, which provided theoretical support for the construction of the lignocellulosic pretreatment process. Liu et al. proposed that the recycling of DES has always been controversial, because its recycling process is complex, and the efficiency of DES after recycling decreases with the increase of the recycling cycle [70]. Antisovent addition, membrane separation, and electrodialysis are common means of separating and recovering DES after fractionation of biomass, however, they do not seem to be a good option in terms of cost and ease of use [71]. Simple recycling methods such as filtration and centrifugation cannot separate the lignin dissolved in DES, which significantly affects the pretreatment performance of DES after recovery. Therefore, how to remove impurities while maintaining the original performance of DES is a problem that needs to be solved at present.

International Journal of Biological Macromolecules 306 (2025) 141460 <::logo: Elsevier NON SOLLUS ELSEVIER Stylized tree with a figure on each side, a serpent, and text above and below the tree.::> Contents lists available at ScienceDirect International Journal of Biological Macromolecules journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/ijbiomac <::logo: Elsevier INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF Biological Macromolecules STRUCTURE, FUNCTION AND INTERACTIONS ScienceDirect Green background with a white outline of a biological macromolecule.::> <::logo: Check for updates A circular icon with a red banner and blue and yellow elements, over text "Check for updates".::> Exploration of biomass fractionation and lignin removal for enhancing enzymatic digestion of wheat-stalk through deep eutectic solvent Cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride:Lactic acid treatment Ying Chen⁰, Zhengyu Tang⁰, Wei Tang⁰, Cuiluan Maⁱ, Yu-Cai He⁰,* ª *School of Pharmacy & Biological and Food Engineering, Changzhou University, Changzhou 213164, China* b *State Key Laboratory of Biocatalysis and Enzyme Engineering, Hubei University, Wuhan 430062, China* ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Lignocellulose pretreatment Delignification Enzymolysis ABSTRACT The cationic surfactant-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted extensive attention due to their effectual destruction of the natural anti-degradation barrier structure in lignocellulose. In this research, functional DES Cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride: Lactic acid (CTAC:LA molar ratio 1:0.5 to 1:6) was fabricated for pretreating wheat-stalk. The relationships of accessibility, lignin removal, xylan separation, and enzymolysis efficiency were explored. The highest delignification (88.3%) and xylan removal (89.0%) were obtained through the treatment with CTAC:LA (1:4, mol/mol, 160 °C, 60 min), acquiring 86.8% of enzymolysis efficiency. The structure of CTAC:LA-treated wheat-stalk was changed to porous state, while the accessibility and crystallinity were substantially improved to 668.2 mg/g and 57.6%, respectively. The lignin surface area declined from 672.7 to 335.4 m²/g. Furthermore, the structure of lignin disrupted by CTAC:LA was analyzed by 2D-HSQC NMR, implying that CTAC:LA could cleave the C-O covalent bond and C-C bond and degrade the S- and H-units in wheat-stalk lignin through interaction. The potential pretreatment mechanism was proposed through comprehensive exploration at the molecular level and macro level, and this built pretreatment process held great promise for valorizing biomass into highly valuable chemicals. ## 1. Introduction Under the double pressure of global energy crisis and environmental pollution issue, seeking effectual and eco-friendly energy production mode has become a research hotspot in modern society [1]. Wheat-stalk (WS) is a common agricultural waste, rendering as an important feed-stock for producing chemicals and fuels in biorefinery [2,3]. However, in the complex structure of WS, lignin combines with hemicelluloses to fabricate the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC), shielding cellulose accessible surface, blocking the cell wall deconstruction and hindering enzymolysis [4]. Distinct from cellulose and lignin, hemicellulose is prone to degradation under high temperature [5]. Lignin is known as a polyphenol biomacromolecule with complex structure [6]. It has a random three-dimensional structure formed by covalent cross-linking of multiple subunits, and the complexity of these connections makes lignin difficult to degrade [7,8]. Consequently, it is of great significance to disrupt lignin and hemicellulose in lignocellulose through efficient pretreatment, greatly improving its enzymolysis efficiency. In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs), which can be fabricated by mixing hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD), have gained extensive attentions as a new green solvent for breaking down and hydrolyzing LCC through the disruption of the existing bonding interactions between carbohydrates and lignin [9,10]. Alvarez-Vasco et al. used four DESs (ChCl:Lactic acid, ChCl:Acetic acid, ChCl:Levulinic acid, and ChCl:Glycerol) for extraction of lignin in poplar wood. Among all four DESs, ChCl:Lactic acid had the greatest effect on lignin removal [11]. It has been reported that the enhanced lignin removal effect of ChCl:Lactic acid could be attributed to the high hydrogen bond supply capacity of lactic acid (LA), which makes the ether bonds in lignin easy to crack during the removal of lignin [12]. Recently, cationic surfactants with hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties have been used to reduce surface tension of lignocellulose driving the removal of hydrophobic molecules such as lignin, thus affecting the enzymolysis efficiency of lignocellulose [13], and they were used to synthesize DESs for removing lignin and enhancing enzymatic saccharification. Using CTAB and ethylene glycol to synthesize DES for the pre- treatment of rape straw, the lignin removal reached 62.2%, resulting in a 46.0% of enzymolysis efficiency [15]. However, the pretreatment ability of CTAB-based DES containing Br- is not ideal, and exploring high efficiency of surfactant-based DES for efficiently removing lignin and promoting enzymolysis has gained great attention. In addition, the corresponding mechanism for lignin elimination and enhanced enzy- molysis through the DES pretreatment need to be well interpreted. It has been reported that the supplementary of CI- into the pre-treatment system can significantly increase the lignin elimination [9,16] and destroy lignocellulose structure [17]. In addition, chloride can participate in stabilizing the protonation transition state of the acid-catalyzed reaction [18]. Therefore, cationic surfactant-based DESS containing CI- group might be efficiently used for efficient biomass pretreatment and valorization. Accordingly, cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride (CTAC), as CI--contained surfactant, was utilized as HBA to fabricate novel surfactant-based DES CTAC:LA by using lactic acid (LA) as HBD, which was used as an eco-friendly and efficient solvent for WS pretreatment in this research. The impact of pretreatment parameters such as DES CTAC:LA solvent properties, CTAC-to-LA molar ratio, pre-treatment temperature, and pretreatment duration on biomass frac-tionation efficiency were assessed. Meanwhile, the contents of furfural and XOSs and the effects of reaction severity factors on their formation were analyzed. The alterations in the chemical composition, surface microstructure, crystal structure, accessibility, and surface lignin area of WS through the CTAC:LA treatment were interpreted by a range of characterization methods (XRD, SEM, dye adsorption techniques, etc.). Additionally, two-dimensional heteronuclear single quantum coherent nuclear magnetic resonance (2D-HSQC NMR) was applied to analyze the changes of lignin structure. The CTAC:LA treatment mechanism for enhancing the enzymolysis of WS was explored and discussed. These efforts comprehensively elaborated the CTAC:LA treatment mechanism, deepened the understanding of the structural characteristics of lignin, and provided scientific basis for promoting lignocellulose pretreatment efficiency in biorefining. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Chemicals and materials The wheat-stalk (WS) used in the experiment was collected from Jiangsu, China. The substrates were ground to 20–60 mesh. Cetyl tri- methyl ammonium chloride (CTAC) were purchased from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co. Ltd. Lactic acid (AR) and other chemicals were sourced from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., LTD. 2.2. Preparation of *CTAC:LA* and related parameters DES was fabricated by cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride (HBA) and lactic acid (HBD) at different HBA:HBD molar ratios (from 1:0.5 to 1:6), the surface tension was measured with surface tensimeter (KINO A201, U.S.A.), the viscosity was measured with rotary viscometer (Brookfield A1017, U.S.A.), and the average was repeated three times. The synthesis of DES (CTAC:LA) was verified by FT-IR. The hydrogen bond capacity of DESs was quantified by Kamlet-Taft solvation parameters, and hydrogen bond donor capacity (α), hydrogen bond acceptor capacity (β), and polarity/polarizability (π*) were determined as previously described [19]. 2.3. Pretreatment and chemical composition analysis of WS DES and WS were mixed at a specific solid-liquid mass ratio (1:15) in a 250-mL flask, which was immersed in oil bath. The pretreatment was implemented with DES (molar ratio of HBA-to-HBD 1:0.5-1:6) at a designed reaction temperature (120 °C-200 °C) for a certain pretreat- ment duration (20 min-100 min). The pretreatment severity factor (LogR0) serves as a comprehensive parameter for assessing the intensity of biomass pretreatment processes, and this factor typically considers the effects of temperature and time during pretreatment on reaction strength. It has proven to be an effective tool for comparing and pre- dicting the performance of various pretreatment strategies in terms of hemicellulose dissolution and lignin removal [20]. Based on the given reaction temperature (T) and time (t), LogR0 (the severity factor) was defined according to Eq. (1). The pretreated WS samples obtained from the different severity factor were used for chemical composition analysis and enzymolysis. The degree of the recovery of solid (Rs), removal of xylan (Rx), and delignification (D) were calculated as below: Rs (%) = (Pretreated WS (g) / Unpretreated WS (g)) × 100 (2) D (%) = (1 - (Lignin in pretreated WS (g) / Lignin in unpretreated WS (g))) × 100 (3) Rx (%) = (1 - (Xylan in pretreated WS (g) / Xylan in unpretreated WS (g))) × 100 (4) 2.4. *Enzymolysis of WS* Raw WS or WS after pretreatment were hydrolyzed with cellulase (10 FPU/g-glucan) in citric acid buffer solution (pH 4.8, 50 mM) to test enzymolysis efficiency. The hydrolysis reaction was implemented at 50 °C for 72 h. The supernatant was subsequently sampled to determine the monosaccharide content. Enzymolysis efficiency (EE) was calculated using the following formula: EE (%) = ([Glucose] + [cellobiose] in enzymatic hydrolysate (g) × 0.9) / (Glucan in pretreated WS (g)) × 100 (5) 2.5. *Quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations* To gain a deeper understanding of the interactions between the typical structural units [S- (syringyl), G- (guaiacyl), and H- (p-hydroxyphenyl) types] of WS lignin and CTAC:LA solvent systems, the interaction types were visually differentiated based on the independent gradient model (IGM) in density functional theory (DFT) to reveal the strong non-covalent interactions between atoms or molecules in the system [21]. Additionally, visual molecular dynamics (VMD) was utilized to draw electrostatic potential (ESP) and other color mapping isosurfaces to visualize the trajectory data of the system [22]. 2.6. Langmuir nonlinear fitting was used to assess the maximum dye adsorption capacity of biomass samples and evaluate its lignocellulose accessibility and lignin surface area [27]. 2.7.2. FT-IR, XRD and SEM FT-IR was applied to observe the structural difference of the com- pound molecules in the range of 4000–500 cm⁻¹, and the analysis was performed on instrument (Thermo Fisher Nicolet IS50) using the KBr pressure tablet method. The structure and morphology of the WS sam- ples were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (JSM- 6360LA, Japan), the surface of the WS sample was sprayed with gold and imaged at 5 kV. The crystallinity was measured by X-ray diffrac- tometer (XRD) (SmartLab SE, Rigaku, Japan) with diffraction angles ranging from 5° to 80°. The crystallinity index (CrI) was calculated [28]. ## 2.8. Recovery and reuse of the DES The recycling ability of DES is an important index of its biomass pretreatment performance [14]. Firstly, WS was pretreated with CTAC: LA (HBA:HBD molar ratio = 1:4) at 160 °C at a 1:15 of solid-liquid mass ratio for 60 min. After the reaction, the pretreated liquid was filtered using filter bottle and Brinell funnel. Then the filtrate was repeatedly used as a solvent for the next run of pretreatment, which was carried out under the same biomass conditions. The filter residue was rinsed and utilized for subsequent component analysis and enzymolysis. 2.9. _Statistical analysis_ All the pretreatment and enzymolysis experiments were implemented in triplicate to confirm the reproducibility of the data. The SPSS software was utilized for the analysis of variance (ANOVA) to test for statistically significant differences. ### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Investigation of HBA:HBD molar ratio on affecting the enzymolysis The molar ratio of HBA to HBD in DES can affect the solubility and selective dissolution of biomass components [29]. It was found that the total lignin content (acid-soluble lignin + acid-insoluble lignin) reached 14.6 % (Fig. 1a), the lignin removal only reached 51.4 %, and the enzymolysis efficiency was 49.4 % after CTAC:LA (HBA:HBD = 1:0.5, 160 °C, 60 min) treatment (Fig. 1b). It was reported that a low pro-portion of HBD couldn't form effective hydrogen-bond network and resulted in increased viscosity and reduced fluidity of the solvent, which would impact the dissolution efficiency between the solvent and biomass [30]. When the CTAC-to-LA molar ratio reached 1:4, the xylan removal (89.0 %) and lignin removal (88.3 %) reached their highest value, acquiring 86.8 % of enzymolysis efficiency. As the CTAC-to-LA molar ratio continued to increase to 1:6, the lignin removal showed a weak downward trend (from 88.3 % to 86.5 %), and the enzymolysis efficiency also declined correspondingly (Fig. 1b). Simultaneously, it has been demonstrated that the molar ratio of HBA to HBD significantly impacted the enzymolysis efficiency through statistical data analysis (p < 0.05) (Table S1, see supplementary file). Continuing to increase the molar ratio of HBA:HBD might improve the polarity of DESs and weaken its interaction with non-polar or hydrophobic biomass components, such as lignin, thereby reducing DES's ability to dissolve lignocellulose [31]. Therefore, CTAC:LA = 1:4 was considered the most appropriate HBA: HBD molar ratio. By using LA as HBD, the absorption peak of LA's carboxyl group was red-shifted, as shown in FT-IR spectra. Meanwhile, the bending vibra-tion of quaternary ammonium cation in CTAC also changed (Fig. S1, see supplementary file). The frequency shift and intensity changes of the representative bands of CTAC and LA in FT-IR spectra confirmed the existence of molecular hydrogen bonds between CTAC and LA [32], implying the successful synthesis of DES. The Kamlet-Taft solvation parameters of DES solvent can be used to evaluate its solubility [33]. With increasing the molar ratio of HBA:HBD, the π* value remained between 0.20 and 0.27, the β value of the solvent (Lewis alkalinity) remained between 1.13 and 1.20, manifesting great hydrogen bond acceptance capacity of CTAC. The α value of the solvent (Lewis acidity) elevated from 0.36 to 1.77, and the hydrogen bond donor capacity changed with the HBA:HBD molar ratio (from 1:0.5 to 1:6) (Table S2, see supplementary file). It was also found that there were fittings about the α value and the solubility of lignin and xylan. As displayed in Fig. 1c, the xylan removal [Y(Xylan removal) = 46.93 × X(Hydrogen bond acidity) + 31.12, R² = 0.86] and delignification [Y(Delignification) = 39.34 × X(Hydrogen bond acidity) + 39.76, R² = 0.91] were positively correlated with the α value of DES. Higher α value in the solvent facilitated the elimination of lignin and xylan because it might enhance the hydrogen-bond interaction be-tween the solvent and lignocellulose, making it easier for the lignin and xylan to dissociate from the biomass complex [34]. The viscosity and surface tension of the solvent can directly affect its diffusion rate and permeability in lignocellulosic pores [35]. CTAC is a cationic surfactant with molecular structure that includes hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail, giving it the ability to reduce surface tension [36]. As showcased in Table 1, solvent systems with different CTAC:LA molar ratios all exhibited low surface tension (29.1–30.9 mN/m), which facilitated CTAC:LA in effectually wetting solid surfaces, penetrating biomass fibers more easily, and promoting the separation of lignocellulosic components. When the CTAC:LA molar ratio reached 1:2, the high viscosity (1223.1 cP) limited the effective contact between the solvent and the biomass. As the molar ratio of CTAC:LA was increased to 1:4, the viscosity was reduced to 380.9 cP, and the removal of lignin and xylan elevated apparently. This was because DESs with lower viscosity could penetrate into the biomass structure more quickly, improving mass transfer performance and efficiency [37]. 3.2. Investigation of CTAC:LA treatment under the different severity factor The severity factor of pretreatment plays decisive role in the overall effectiveness of the pretreatment [38]. Accordingly, the impact of two key parameters in the severity factor (pretreatment temperature and duration) on the pretreatment effectiveness was assessed and optimized. 3 Y. Chen et al. Molecular dynamics simulation Molecular dynamics simulation is able to render atomic and molec-ular level insights by simulating the interactions between substrate and solvent molecules [50]. In this research, the interactions between the CTAC:LA treatment system and lignin were discussed by molecular dy-namics simulation. The lignin in WS is a typical S-G-H type lignin (Syringyl-Guaiacyl-p-Hydroxyphenyl lignin). To further understand the interaction between the lignin unit and the CTAC:LA treatment system, the weak interaction between the CTAC:LA and the lignin structure was visualized. Van der Waals forces, which mainly include electrostatic interaction, induction force and dispersion force, might promote the interaction between pretreatment solvents and non-polar or hydropho- bic compounds in lignocellulose, and promote their degradation [51]. Mass flow and energy flow Lignocellulose can be effectually transformed into fermentable sugars and other bio-based products through efficient pretreatment and enzymolysis [62,63]. In this research, 1000 g WS composed of 417.3 g glucan, 165.0 g xylan, 162.3 g acid-insoluble lignin, and 15.0 g acid-soluble lignin was used as raw material for biorefining. After CTAC:LA fractionation, the cellulose-rich solid residue consisting of 212.0 g glucan, 18.1 g xylan, 17.2 g acid-insoluble lignin, and 3.4 g acid-soluble lignin was recovered. The removal of xylan was 89.0 % and the lignin removal reached 88.3 %. In the pretreatment liquid, 38.9 g furfural and 34.0 g xylo-oligosaccharides were produced. After enzymolysis of the cellulose-rich solid residue, 201.9 g glucose, 2.5 g cellobiose, 14.5 g xylose, 1.1 g arabinose were released (Fig. 8a). These sugars are important bio-based products that can be used in subsequent biotransformation processes. To explore the potential applications of this biorefining pathway, the overall energy flow was further evaluated (Fig. 8b). The energy flow image manifested that the high calorific value (HHV) of WS consists of glucan (7.26 MJ/kg WS), xylan (2.87 MJ/kg WS), and lignin (4.26 MJ/kg WS). Throughout the entire biorefining process of WS (1000 g), the energy output of furfural, XOSs, and lignin-enriched products reached 0.91, 0.60, and 5.30 MJ respectively. The majority of carbohydrate energy has been successfully converted into value-added forms, demonstrating the potential industrial application. Despite the remarkable progress in the biomass utilization and conversion process, the generation of lignin-enriched products after pretreatment was still an unavoidable problem. Lignin has the potential for many applications [64]. Li et al. found that the lignin regenerated from the acid DES (ChCl:oxalic acid) pretreatment solution had good thermal stability and antioxidant activity [65]. In addition, Liu et al. showed that biobased plastics prepared with recycled lignin from the pretreatment solution have better mechanical and tensile strength [66]. Therefore, these lignin-rich products generated in the CTAC:LA pretreatment system provide unlimited possibilities for further processing and upgrading into high value-added products (such as antioxidants, heat stabilizers, and plastics). 3.8. _Potential CTAC:LA pretreatment mechanism_ Effective pretreatment of WS was realized through the action of DES (CTAC:LA), and its potential pretreatment mechanism was illustrated in Fig. 9. As a carboxylic acid with high hydrogen bond donor capacity, lactic acid might provide large numbers of protons for efficient elimi- nation of hemicellulose and lignin [12]. CTAC, a surfactant with hy- drophobic long alkyl chain structure, not only affected the hydrophobic lignin structure but also could prevent the decomposed lignin molecules from recondensing into pseudo-lignin and being deposited on the biomass surface [53]. Under the action of CTAC:LA treatment system, a large number of lignin and xylan were eliminated from the WS structure, which substantially elevated the accessibility and crystallinity of WS after treatment, and reduced the lignin surface area, thus advancing the subsequent enzymolysis efficiency (Fig. 9). Through quantum chemistry calculation and molecular dynamics simulation, it was found that there was strong and weak interaction (mainly van der Waals forces and hydrogen bond interaction) between lignin model and CTAC:LA treat- ment system. These interactions lead to the weakened connections be- tween lignin, hemicellulose and cellulose, and the S-units, H-units, C—O (β-0-4) covalent and C—C (β-5, β-β) bonds in the lignin were effectually cleaved by CTAC:LA, promoting the removal of lignin and thereby enhancing the enzymolysis of carbohydrates. The key to making the most of lignocellulose and achieving an environmentally sustainable future lies in effective pretreatment strategies [67-69]. In this research, CTAC containing CI- was used as hydrogen bond receptor to synthesize a new type of cationic surfactant-based DES (CTAC:LA). This system could efficiently remove lignin and xylan from WS, significantly improve the accessibility and crystallinity of WS after pretreatment and make the substrate after pretreatment show excellent enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency (86.8%). This provided favorable conditions for the conversion of biomass into high-value chemicals. In addition, various characterizations combined with molecular simulation revealed the potential pretreatment mechanism of cationic surfactant-based DES, which provided theoretical support for the construction of the lignocellulosic pretreatment process. Liu et al. proposed that the recycling of DES has always been controversial, because its recycling process is complex, and the efficiency of DES after recycling decreases with the increase of the recycling cycle [70]. Antisovent addition, membrane separation, and electrodialysis are common means of separating and recovering DES after fractionation of biomass, however, they do not seem to be a good option in terms of cost and ease of use [71]. Simple recycling methods such as filtration and centrifugation cannot separate the lignin dissolved in DES, which significantly affects the pretreatment performance of DES after recovery. Therefore, how to remove impurities while maintaining the original performance of DES is a problem that needs to be solved at present. ## 4. In this research, functional DES Cetyl trimethyl ammonium chloride: Lactic acid (CTAC:LA molar ratio 1:0.5 to 1:6) was fabricated for pretreating wheat-stalk. The relationships of accessibility, lignin removal, xylan separation, and enzymolysis efficiency were explored. The highest delignification (88.3%) and xylan removal (89.0%) were obtained through the treatment with CTAC:LA (1:4, mol/mol, 160 °C, 60 min), acquiring 86.8% of enzymolysis efficiency. The structure of CTAC:LA-treated wheat-stalk was changed to porous state, while the accessibility and crystallinity were substantially improved to 668.2 mg/g and 57.6%, respectively. The lignin surface area declined from 672.7 to 335.4 m²/g. Furthermore, the structure of lignin disrupted by CTAC:LA was analyzed by 2D-HSQC NMR, implying that CTAC:LA could cleave the C-O covalent bond and C-C bond and degrade the S- and H-units in wheat-stalk lignin through interaction. Introduction Under the double pressure of global energy crisis and environmental pollution issue, seeking effectual and eco-friendly energy production mode has become a research hotspot in modern society [1]. Wheat-stalk (WS) is a common agricultural waste, rendering as an important feed-stock for producing chemicals and fuels in biorefinery [2,3]. However, in the complex structure of WS, lignin combines with hemicelluloses to fabricate the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC), shielding cellulose accessible surface, blocking the cell wall deconstruction and hindering enzymolysis [4]. Distinct from cellulose and lignin, hemicellulose is prone to degradation under high temperature [5]. Lignin is known as a polyphenol biomacromolecule with complex structure [6]. It has a random three-dimensional structure formed by covalent cross-linking of multiple subunits, and the complexity of these connections makes lignin difficult to degrade [7,8]. Consequently, it is of great significance to disrupt lignin and hemicellulose in lignocellulose through efficient pretreatment, greatly improving its enzymolysis efficiency. In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs), which can be fabricated by mixing hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD), have gained extensive attentions as a new green solvent for breaking down and hydrolyzing LCC through the disruption of the existing bonding interactions between carbohydrates and lignin [9,10]. Alvarez-Vasco et al. used four DESs (ChCl:Lactic acid, ChCl:Acetic acid, ChCl:Levulinic acid, and ChCl:Glycerol) for extraction of lignin in poplar wood. Among all four DESs, ChCl:Lactic acid had the greatest effect on lignin removal [11]. It has been reported that the enhanced lignin removal effect of ChCl:Lactic acid could be attributed to the high hydrogen bond supply capacity of lactic acid (LA), which makes the ether bonds in lignin easy to crack during the removal of lignin [12]. Recently, cationic surfactants with hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties have been used to reduce surface tension of lignocellulose driving the removal of hydrophobic molecules such as lignin, thus affecting the enzymolysis efficiency of lignocellulose [13], and they were used to synthesize DESs for removing lignin and enhancing enzymatic saccharification. Investigation of HBA:HBD molar ratio on affecting the enzymolysis The molar ratio of HBA to HBD in DES can affect the solubility and selective dissolution of biomass components [29]. It was found that the total lignin content (acid-soluble lignin + acid-insoluble lignin) reached 14.6 % (Fig. 1a), the lignin removal only reached 51.4 %, and the enzymolysis efficiency was 49.4 % after CTAC:LA (HBA:HBD = 1:0.5, 160 °C, 60 min) treatment (Fig. 1b). It was reported that a low pro-portion of HBD couldn't form effective hydrogen-bond network and resulted in increased viscosity and reduced fluidity of the solvent, which would impact the dissolution efficiency between the solvent and biomass [30]. When the CTAC-to-LA molar ratio reached 1:4, the xylan removal (89.0 %) and lignin removal (88.3 %) reached their highest value, acquiring 86.8 % of enzymolysis efficiency. As the CTAC-to-LA molar ratio continued to increase to 1:6, the lignin removal showed a weak downward trend (from 88.3 % to 86.5 %), and the enzymolysis efficiency also declined correspondingly (Fig. 1b). Simultaneously, it has been demonstrated that the molar ratio of HBA to HBD significantly impacted the enzymolysis efficiency through statistical data analysis (p < 0.05) (Table S1, see supplementary file). Continuing to increase the molar ratio of HBA:HBD might improve the polarity of DESs and weaken its interaction with non-polar or hydrophobic biomass components, such as lignin, thereby reducing DES's ability to dissolve lignocellulose [31]. Therefore, CTAC:LA = 1:4 was considered the most appropriate HBA: HBD molar ratio. By using LA as HBD, the absorption peak of LA's carboxyl group was red-shifted, as shown in FT-IR spectra. Meanwhile, the bending vibra-tion of quaternary ammonium cation in CTAC also changed (Fig. S1, see supplementary file). The frequency shift and intensity changes of the representative bands of CTAC and LA in FT-IR spectra confirmed the existence of molecular hydrogen bonds between CTAC and LA [32], implying the successful synthesis of DES. The Kamlet-Taft solvation parameters of DES solvent can be used to evaluate its solubility [33]. With increasing the molar ratio of HBA:HBD, the π* value remained between 0.20 and 0.27, the β value of the solvent (Lewis alkalinity) remained between 1.13 and 1.20, manifesting great hydrogen bond acceptance capacity of CTAC. The α value of the solvent (Lewis acidity) elevated from 0.36 to 1.77, and the hydrogen bond donor capacity changed with the HBA:HBD molar ratio (from 1:0.5 to 1:6) (Table S2, see supplementary file). It was also found that there were fittings about the α value and the solubility of lignin and xylan. Higher α value in the solvent facilitated the elimination of lignin and xylan because it might enhance the hydrogen-bond interaction be-tween the solvent and lignocellulose, making it easier for the lignin and xylan to dissociate from the biomass complex [34]. The viscosity and surface tension of the solvent can directly affect its diffusion rate and permeability in lignocellulosic pores [35]. CTAC is a cationic surfactant with molecular structure that includes hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail, giving it the ability to reduce surface tension [36]. As showcased in Table 1, solvent systems with different CTAC:LA molar ratios all exhibited low surface tension (29.1–30.9 mN/m), which facilitated CTAC:LA in effectually wetting solid surfaces, penetrating biomass fibers more easily, and promoting the separation of lignocellulosic components. Molecular dynamics simulation Molecular dynamics simulation is able to render atomic and molec-ular level insights by simulating the interactions between substrate and solvent molecules [50]. In this research, the interactions between the CTAC:LA treatment system and lignin were discussed by molecular dy-namics simulation. The lignin in WS is a typical S-G-H type lignin (Syringyl-Guaiacyl-p-Hydroxyphenyl lignin). To further understand the interaction between the lignin unit and the CTAC:LA treatment system, the weak interaction between the CTAC:LA and the lignin structure was visualized. Van der Waals forces, which mainly include electrostatic interaction, induction force and dispersion force, might promote the interaction between pretreatment solvents and non-polar or hydropho- bic compounds in lignocellulose, and promote their degradation [51]. In molecular simulations, electrostatic interactions can be evaluated by electrostatic potential. Among the three lignin structural models, G-type lignin model molecules manifested the strongest electrostatic interac- tion with DES, since the lowest self-electrostatic potential value of -0.961 (Fig. 5a). Analysis of crystallinity The crystallinity of lignocellulose is believed to play a crucial role in the conversion of lignocellulose into fermentable sugars [60]. Mass flow and energy flow Lignocellulose can be effectually transformed into fermentable sugars and other bio-based products through efficient pretreatment and enzymolysis [62,63]. In this research, 1000 g WS composed of 417.3 g glucan, 165.0 g xylan, 162.3 g acid-insoluble lignin, and 15.0 g acid-soluble lignin was used as raw material for biorefining. After CTAC:LA fractionation, the cellulose-rich solid residue consisting of 212.0 g glucan, 18.1 g xylan, 17.2 g acid-insoluble lignin, and 3.4 g acid-soluble lignin was recovered. The removal of xylan was 89.0 % and the lignin removal reached 88.3 %. In the pretreatment liquid, 38.9 g furfural and 34.0 g xylo-oligosaccharides were produced. After enzymolysis of the cellulose-rich solid residue, 201.9 g glucose, 2.5 g cellobiose, 14.5 g xylose, 1.1 g arabinose were released (Fig. 8a). These sugars are important bio-based products that can be used in subsequent biotransformation processes. To explore the potential applications of this biorefining pathway, the overall energy flow was further evaluated (Fig. 8b). The energy flow image manifested that the high calorific value (HHV) of WS consists of glucan (7.26 MJ/kg WS), xylan (2.87 MJ/kg WS), and lignin (4.26 MJ/kg WS). Throughout the entire biorefining process of WS (1000 g), the energy output of furfural, XOSs, and lignin-enriched products reached 0.91, 0.60, and 5.30 MJ respectively. The majority of carbohydrate energy has been successfully converted into value-added forms, demonstrating the potential industrial application. Despite the remarkable progress in the biomass utilization and conversion process, the generation of lignin-enriched products after pretreatment was still an unavoidable problem. Lignin has the potential for many applications [64]. Li et al. found that the lignin regenerated from the acid DES (ChCl:oxalic acid) pretreatment solution had good thermal stability and antioxidant activity [65]. In addition, Liu et al. showed that biobased plastics prepared with recycled lignin from the pretreatment solution have better mechanical and tensile strength [66]. Therefore, these lignin-rich products generated in the CTAC:LA pretreatment system provide unlimited possibilities for further processing and upgrading into high value-added products (such as antioxidants, heat stabilizers, and plastics). 3.8. _Potential CTAC:LA pretreatment mechanism_ Effective pretreatment of WS was realized through the action of DES (CTAC:LA), and its potential pretreatment mechanism was illustrated in Fig. 9. As a carboxylic acid with high hydrogen bond donor capacity, lactic acid might provide large numbers of protons for efficient elimi- nation of hemicellulose and lignin [12]. CTAC, a surfactant with hy- drophobic long alkyl chain structure, not only affected the hydrophobic lignin structure but also could prevent the decomposed lignin molecules from recondensing into pseudo-lignin and being deposited on the biomass surface [53]. Under the action of CTAC:LA treatment system, a large number of lignin and xylan were eliminated from the WS structure, which substantially elevated the accessibility and crystallinity of WS after treatment, and reduced the lignin surface area, thus advancing the subsequent enzymolysis efficiency (Fig. 9). Through quantum chemistry calculation and molecular dynamics simulation, it was found that there was strong and weak interaction (mainly van der Waals forces and hydrogen bond interaction) between lignin model and CTAC:LA treat- ment system. These interactions lead to the weakened connections be- tween lignin, hemicellulose and cellulose, and the S-units, H-units, C—O (β-0-4) covalent and C—C (β-5, β-β) bonds in the lignin were effectually cleaved by CTAC:LA, promoting the removal of lignin and thereby enhancing the enzymolysis of carbohydrates. The key to making the most of lignocellulose and achieving an environmentally sustainable future lies in effective pretreatment strategies [67-69]. In this research, CTAC containing CI- was used as hydrogen bond receptor to synthesize a new type of cationic surfactant-based DES (CTAC:LA). This system could efficiently remove lignin and xylan from WS, significantly improve the accessibility and crystallinity of WS after pretreatment and make the substrate after pretreatment show excellent enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency (86.8%). This provided favorable conditions for the conversion of biomass into high-value chemicals. In addition, various characterizations combined with molecular simulation revealed the potential pretreatment mechanism of cationic surfactant-based DES, which provided theoretical support for the construction of the lignocellulosic pretreatment process. Liu et al. proposed that the recycling of DES has always been controversial, because its recycling process is complex, and the efficiency of DES after recycling decreases with the increase of the recycling cycle [70]. Antisovent addition, membrane separation, and electrodialysis are common means of separating and recovering DES after fractionation of biomass, however, they do not seem to be a good option in terms of cost and ease of use [71]. Simple recycling methods such as filtration and centrifugation cannot separate the lignin dissolved in DES, which significantly affects the pretreatment performance of DES after recovery. Therefore, how to remove impurities while maintaining the original performance of DES is a problem that needs to be solved at present. ## 4.
